record.paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
record.context_brief: Relative roles of environmental galaxy-evolution processes
record.original_question: How do environmental processes such as ram-pressure stripping, harassment, strangulation, tidal stripping, and assembly bias combine through interacting actions, back-reactions, and self-regulation to produce the observed detailed trends in satellite galaxy properties, and how can the relative role of each physical process be quantified?

evidence.quote: Question 4 - We understand which processes affect galaxies in different environments. Do the details matter?

we know which processes affect the evolution of satellite galaxies (ram-pressure, harassment, strangulation, tidal stripping, and assembly bias are all at work), we certainly do not understand how these processes combine to establish the detailed trends we observe.

Therefore, the obvious answer to this question is: yes, the details do matter because, in order to understand how galaxies evolve in different environments, we need to quantify the relative role of different physical processes.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Satellite galaxies in groups and clusters are subject to several environmental physical processes that alter their gas content, star-formation activity, morphology, and structural properties. The principal processes are: (i) ram-pressure stripping, the removal of cold interstellar gas by the hydrodynamic pressure of the hot intracluster/intragroup medium as a galaxy moves through it; (ii) galaxy harassment, the cumulative effect of many high-speed gravitational encounters with other group/cluster members; (iii) strangulation (or starvation), the removal or cutoff of the extended hot gas reservoir that would otherwise cool and replenish the disk, halting future star formation; (iv) tidal stripping, the removal of stars and dark matter from the outer regions of a satellite by the tidal field of the host halo or of nearby galaxies; and (v) assembly bias, the dependence of galaxy properties on the assembly history of the host dark-matter halo at fixed halo mass.

These processes do not act independently: each can trigger, suppress, amplify, or be modified by the others through back-reactions, and the resulting evolution is self-regulating. Provide a quantitative framework that:

(a) Describes how these five processes combine—through their interactions, back-reactions, and self-regulation—to produce the observed statistical trends in satellite galaxy properties (such as quenched fractions, gas fractions, colors, morphologies, sizes, and stellar-to-halo mass relations) as functions of host halo mass, halocentric distance, infall time, and stellar mass.

(b) Quantifies the relative contribution of each individual process to those trends, in such a way that the contributions can be disentangled from observations and from cosmological simulations.

In particular, derive or specify observables and estimators that uniquely separate the signatures of ram-pressure stripping, harassment, strangulation, tidal stripping, and assembly bias on the satellite population.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a broad open question in galaxy formation. Disentangling the relative contributions of ram-pressure stripping, harassment, strangulation, tidal stripping, and assembly bias on satellite galaxies remains an active topic; recent works (e.g., on quenching timescales and assembly bias signatures with SDSS/DESI and IllustrisTNG/EAGLE simulations) provide partial constraints but no unified quantitative decomposition has been established.

status_evidence.title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution?
status_evidence.snippet: Question 4 ... we certainly do not understand how these processes combine to establish the detailed trends we observe.
status_evidence.claim: The question is posed as an open problem in galaxy evolution.
